The proposed solution asserts that the exponent is $c = 3/4$. 

However, under the canonical one-factor equicorrelated Gaussian copula model, the $p$-values are generated as $p_k = \Phi(Z_k)$ with $Z_k = \sqrt{\rho_K} Z_0 + \sqrt{1 - \rho_K} \epsilon_k$, where $Z_0, \epsilon_1, \dots, \epsilon_K \stackrel{i.i.d.}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$. 

The tail behavior of the Cauchy combination test statistic is dominated by the extreme $p$-values (specifically, the minimum $p$-value $p_{(1)}$). From Gaussian extreme value theory, the extremes of $K$ standard normal variables scale as $\sqrt{2 \log K}$. Expanding the underlying Gaussian variable gives:
$$Z_{(1)} \approx -\sqrt{2 \log K}\sqrt{1 - \rho_K} + \sqrt{\rho_K} Z_0$$
The tail probability $\Phi(Z_{(1)})$ depends on $Z_{(1)}^2/2$, where the cross-term and variance shift produce terms proportional to $\rho_K \log K$ and $\sqrt{\rho_K \log K} Z_0$. 

Consequently, the dependence effect vanishes and the test is asymptotically exact if and only if $\rho_K \log K \to 0$, corresponding to $c = 1$, not $3/4$.

VERDICT: REJECT
